newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African minister unfazed by drug firms' threats.
newsitem.headline: S.African minister unfazed by drug firms' threats.

text.p: Health Minister Nkosana Zuma on Thursday predicted that she would win any legal action by pharmaceutical companies to prevent her from implementing plans to make cheaper generic drugs more widely available.

Briefing the media on legislation now before parliament aimed at cutting the cost of drugs, Zuma and her senior officials expressed exasperation about the sudden upsurge of opposition to her plans despite intensive consultation with the industry.
"I have found in this country when you draw up policy, people participate and give inputs and when the policy is launched they accept that is policy," she said.
"But when that policy is being implemented it raises a lot of tempers and anxieties and people forget that they participated in the development of policy."

One of her chief directors, Bada Pharasi, added that the department had consulted the country's two major pharmaceutical manufacturers' organisations and wholesalers on the legislation before it was drafted.
"They agreed, albeit somewhat reluctantly, but they agreed, that it was inevitable that we would have generic substitution," he said.

Asked to comment on reports that pharmaceutical companies were contemplating legal action to block the new legislation, Zuma said that she would obviously prefer they did not go to court as this would delay the introduction of the new regulaions.
"But we are quite confident that we will win eventually even if it goes to court," she said.

Some drug companies have also objected to the fact that drugs sold to the state would not have brand name labels under the new legislation. They claimed that this would infringe their intellectual property rights.
Zuma said the legislation was not aimed at prohibiting the sale of brand name drugs, but more at ensuring that pharmacists informed patients of cheaper, generic medicines available.
"I do not think that there is anything wrong with doing that because many people do not even know the difference between a brand a generic," she said.
